q: You chill a light red to 12°C to serve with charcuterie. What does the temperature drop do to the wine itself?
opts: Blurs the tannin and warms the alcohol
Sharpens acid and tannin, mutes alcohol
Lifts the aromatics and softens the grip
exp: Cold accentuates acidity and astringency and suppresses perceived sweetness, alcohol and aromatic volatility; warmth does the reverse. Temperature is therefore a pairing lever, not just a service convention: chill a fruit-driven red to freshen it against fat and salt, but never chill a genuinely tannic one — you will only make the grip meaner and shut the nose at the same time.

q: Red wine with certain seafood throws a metallic, fishy aftertaste. Name the culprit in the wine and the reaction it drives.
accept: iron catalysing lipid oxidation of the fish oils
ferrous iron oxidises the fish's unsaturated fats into aldehydes
iron in the wine driving oxidation of the fish's polyunsaturated fats
iron content producing fishy aldehydes
ans: Iron — ferrous iron in the wine catalyses oxidation of the seafood's polyunsaturated fatty acids, generating fishy aldehydes; tannin is not the trigger, and a low-iron red pairs cleanly
exp: Japanese work published in 2009 tested wines against dried scallop and found the fishy aftertaste tracked iron content, not tannin, oak or sulphur — adding iron to a harmless wine created the clash, and chelating it removed it. This is why some light reds are fine with tuna and others are foul, and why the practical remedy is a low-iron wine rather than merely a low-tannin one.

q: In the four-element framework (sweetness, umami, salt, acid), what does acidity in the DISH do to the wine, and what is the practical trap?
accept: lowers perceived acidity and makes the wine seem fruitier
the wine tastes softer and rounder so low-acid wines go flabby
food acid flatters high-acid wines and flattens low-acid ones
reduces the wine's apparent acidity increasing fruit and body
ans: Food acid lowers the wine's perceived acidity and lifts its fruit, sweetness and body — flattering a high-acid wine but leaving a low-acid one flabby and dull, so the wine must carry at least as much acid as the plate does
exp: Salt and acid are the two food elements that soften a wine; sugar and umami are the two that harden it. Knowing which way each pushes turns pairing from memorised couples into arithmetic — vinaigrette, ceviche and lemon-dressed fish are opportunities for Sancerre, Assyrtiko or Muscadet, and quiet disasters for a soft, ripe, low-acid Chardonnay.

q: Grilled, smoked and barbecued dishes flatter heavily toasted-oak reds. Name the compound class they share and where each side gets it.
accept: volatile phenols such as guaiacol from smoke and toasted oak
shared volatile phenols guaiacol from lignin in both
guaiacol and other volatile phenols from burnt or toasted wood
volatile phenols made by lignin degradation in smoke and barrel toast
ans: Volatile phenols — guaiacol above all, with syringol and 4-methylguaiacol — released by the breakdown of lignin both in wood smoke and in barrel toasting; the pairing is an aroma-compound echo, not a structural one
exp: A cooper's toasting flame and a smoker's wood pyrolyse the same lignin and release the same phenols, so glass and grill are literally saying one word. Take the general lesson: a bridge pairing works when a compound is genuinely shared, not merely when two things sound rustic together — and note the limit, since these phenols carry no structure, so weight and tannin still have to be matched separately.

q: Describe what astringency physically is, and why a fatty, protein-rich dish reduces it.
accept: tannins precipitate salivary proteins and food protein binds them instead
loss of saliva lubrication as tannin binds proline-rich proteins
astringency is tannin stripping saliva and food protein intercepts it
tannin binds salivary proteins so fat and protein compete for it
ans: Astringency is a loss of lubrication: tannins bind and precipitate the saliva's proline-rich proteins and mucins, so the mouth turns rough and dry. Protein and fat in the food give the tannins something else to bind, and coat the palate, so far less saliva is stripped
exp: Astringency is a tactile event, not a taste — which is the whole reason steak and Cabernet works and the reason a tannic red is at its worst on an empty mouth. It also marks the limit of the trick: protein and fat intercept tannin directly, by binding it, whereas bitterness is a receptor response and answers instead to salt, the most reliable suppressor on the plate.

q: State the classic order-of-service rules for a multi-wine menu, then give two legitimate reversals.
accept: light to heavy dry to sweet young to old but sauternes first with foie gras
the ascending order with a sweet opener and a fragile old wine placed early
dry before sweet light before heavy young before old except foie gras and an old red
sweet last and light first unless sauternes opens or a fading old wine goes early
ans: Dry before sweet, light before full, young before old, simple before fine, white before red. Legitimate reversals: a sweet wine opening the meal with foie gras or a rich pâté, and a fragile mature red served before a powerful young white or a big oaked Chardonnay rather than after it
exp: The rules exist for one reason: so no wine is ambushed by the one poured before it. They are heuristics about contrast rather than laws, which is exactly why they bend — foie gras wants Sauternes at the top of the menu, and a delicate old red is safer ahead of a young powerhouse than behind it. State the rule, then state the exception; that is the Advanced answer.

fino may be unfortified if 15% natural
expanded zone allowed en rama definitions
ans: Permitting unfortified wines at natural 15%+, expanding zones/grapes, formalizing categories
